view: The sūra and al-Mursalāt share an affirmative-question style addressing deniers; each question reproaches them while good news for believers is understood against the warning.
The sūra is Meccan and, in Jābir ibn Zayd's revelation order, follows al-Maʿārij and precedes al-Nāziʿāt.
Medinan, Syrian, and Basran verse counters count forty verses in the sūra; Meccan and Kufan counters count forty-one.
Sky, earth, rain, and plants are pictured as a reproductive pair: sky as male, earth as female, water as semen, and vegetation as offspring; springs and pools are implied.
The signs of creation, including rain, display power and purposeful providence and support the certainty of resurrection, judgment, reward, and punishment.
note: Muqātil calls each sign more astonishing than resurrection; Iṣlāḥī says their mercy, wisdom, and power show humans are accountable.

view: Paired with al-Mursalāt, this sūra uses signs in heaven and earth to establish Judgment as the necessary end of a purposeful world.
note: The account includes reward for the God-fearing and punishment for rebels.

view: The divine plural 'We' signals majesty and the collectivity of the Divine Essence, Names, and Attributes.
For the wind interpretation, min is understood as bi, assigning rain to the winds as its means or cause.
note: The preposition is read instrumentally or causally because the rain itself comes from clouds.

view: With clouds as muʿṣirāt, min marks the source of rain; clouds naturally contain and release water, whereas winds carry or cause it.
note: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās prefer clouds partly on the wording 'from', while allowing that sky is possible.

view: Even with bi-l-muʿṣirāt, clouds can remain the referent: water descends through them, as giving can be expressed with either 'from' or 'by' a hand.
note: This resists treating the variant as decisive for winds.

view: A variant reads bi-l-muʿṣirāt instead of min al-muʿṣirāt; it is attributed to several readers and taken to favor the wind interpretation.
note: The attributions include Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, and Mujāhid. The codices have min; al-Jishumī compares 97:4.

view: A muʿṣir cloud is full of water and near rainfall but has not yet rained, like a young woman nearing menstruation; the form marks an approaching time.
note: The comparison turns on readiness before the flow begins.

view: The cloud name is connected with squeezing water out of clouds, including clouds about to be pressed by winds into rain.
note: The notes also describe clouds as water-laden or already producing rain.

view: The imminence of rain is compared with grain ready for cutting or crops ready for harvest.
note: One note also likens the rain to what is pressed from clouds.

view: Abū al-Najm's verse about a young woman approaching menstruation is cited as evidence for the verb aʿṣarat and the cloud analogy.
note: The poetic citation supports the sense of nearing the relevant time.

view: Authorities dispute when a girl is called muʿṣir: near menstruation, on reaching maturity, approaching twenty, or at the onset of menstruation, when she is confined privately.
note: Al-Azharī reports disagreement with al-Farrāʾ; a cited verse says the girl's period has approached. Ibn al-Aʿrābī also connects ʿaṣr with refuge.

view: Al-Mubarrad explains the cloud as holding water and releasing it little by little; related ʿaṣr words can mean refuge or shelter.
note: This is a distinct derivation from the image of imminent menstruation.

view: Ibn Kaysān relates muʿṣirāt to clouds bringing relief or aid through rain, linking it with the verb in 12:49 about pressing produce.
note: Al-Samīn questions whether the form-IV participle can bear the triliteral verb's sense; al-Zamakhsharī answers that the hamza marks entry into a state of impending relief.

view: The muʿṣirāt can be clouds possessing spiraling or cyclonic winds; the dust whirlwind sense of iʿṣār is offered as linguistic support.
note: Al-Māzinī treats the clouds' cyclonic winds as bringing rain.

view: If winds press clouds, a passive participle with fatḥa on ṣād might be expected for clouds; the imminence sense explains the actual active form.
note: Bursevī rejects a causative analysis for winds because winds themselves do the squeezing.

view: The muʿṣirāt are rain-bearing clouds.
note: Some reports attribute this view to Ibn ʿAbbās as well as to other early authorities; other reports from him identify winds.

view: The muʿṣirāt are winds that bring rain by forming, driving, or pressing clouds.
note: Reports differ over whether Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and others meant winds, clouds, or heaven; the wind view attributes rain to its cause.

view: The muʿṣirāt are the heavens or sky from which water descends.
note: Ibn Kathīr calls this unusual; al-Ālūsī objects that heaven is not squeezed to yield rain.

view: The muʿṣirāt are cyclone-bearing or whirlwind-bearing winds.
note: This specifies the broader wind interpretation.

view: Zayd ibn Aslam specifies the rain-bringing winds as the south wind.
note: This narrows the wind referent.

view: Al-Muʿṣirāt is one of five attested names of the sūra; al-Itqān lists four of those names.
note: The other named forms are al-Nabaʾ, ʿAmma yatasaʾalūn, ʿAmma, and al-Tasāʾul.

view: Al-Azharī favors rain clouds over whirlwind winds because whirlwinds do not carry the abundant rain described here.
note: The disagreement turns on whether the proposed winds bring rain.

view: The sky interpretation can describe water passing from heaven into clouds, with heaven conceived as pressing or enabling the pressing.
note: Al-Naḥḥās allows winds, clouds, and sky to converge in a rain process; al-Ālūsī considers the heaven reconciliation strained.

view: Al-Ālūsī objects to taking muʿṣirāt as the heavens because heaven is not squeezed to produce rain.
note: He calls a proposed reconciliation far-fetched.

view: A report says winds collect water and drive it into clouds until they fill like a milch camel; the water then falls in heavy showers distributed by winds.
note: The notes vary between wind carrying water, clouds filling, and drops resembling water drawn from a pregnant she-camel.

view: Winds are said to carry water from heaven or its lowest sea of provisions into clouds, where it gathers and becomes rain.
note: The wind-water report in al-Samīn is qualified 'if sound'; Muqātil links the heavenly provision to 51:22.

view: Rain may descend through clouds or arise through celestial causes, including the sun lifting water from earth and seas into clouds.
note: This reconciles rain's relation to the sky with its passage through clouds.

view: Rain from the clouds cools the sun's heat and enables food and drink.
note: This is the stated benefit of the water.

view: Pounding, widespread, continuous rain displays harmony between sky and earth and supports monotheism, providence, and accountability.
Muqātil says the Hour cannot come while any water remains, connecting the rain provision to the end of the world.
note: The same note describes clouds and successive rain.

view: Thajjāj describes water pouring or flowing down.
note: The basic gloss is shared across many reports.

view: Thajjāj denotes rain pouring continuously or in successive waves and streams.
note: Some notes specify repeated rain and its abundant benefit.

view: Thajjāj conveys forceful or rushing rain, like blood pouring from a slaughtered animal; one explanation also describes widespread, pounding rain.
note: These notes add force or reach to the general pouring sense.

view: Thajjāj describes plentiful or abundant rain and water.
note: Ibn Zayd is among those glossing it as abundance; al-Qurṭubī regards that as the same sense as pouring.

view: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās reject mere quantity as the Arabic sense of thajj; they prefer repeated, successive pouring, citing the pilgrimage phrase about sacrifice.
note: This disagrees with Ibn Zayd's gloss 'abundant'.

view: Poetry uses thajjāj for a copious, forceful flow or for water pouring from black clouds.
note: These lines are lexical witnesses for heavy flowing rain.

view: Ibn ʿAbbās was called thajjāj because speech poured abundantly from him during sermons.
note: The epithet illustrates the word's use outside rain.

view: A report about prolonged menstrual bleeding uses thajj for repeated, abundant flow.
note: The report is cited as lexical support.

view: Al-Zamakhsharī uses mathājih for water spillways and yantajihu for water flowing into a valley.
note: These related forms illustrate the image of water flowing together.

view: The verb thajja can be intransitive, 'water flowed', or transitive, 'one poured water'; al-Zajjāj takes the water as pouring itself, while al-Ālūsī favors the commoner intransitive sense.
note: The grammatical alternatives both support the image of pouring.

view: Al-Aʿraj reads thajjāḥan with ḥāʾ instead of the written jīm; related mathājiḥ denotes places where water gathers and flows.
note: This is a separate variant of the rain descriptor.

view: A note also reports readings thajjājan and mathājij as terms for outflows.
note: The note places these alongside its gloss of abundant pouring.

view: A Prophetic pilgrimage saying pairs ʿajj, loud talbiya or invocation, with thajj, pouring the blood of sacrificial animals.
note: Some versions call it the best pilgrimage; another asks about an accepted pilgrimage. The phrase is cited to explain thajj, not to derive a ruling here.
